title: Accuracy: agreement, word order and punctuation

units.title: Subject–verb agreement
units.summary: Singular subjects take singular verbs — even when other words get in the way.

cards.title: Find the real subject
cards.body: The verb agrees with the **head noun** of the subject, not with the nearest noun.
examples: The number of students **is** rising.
The quality of the roads **has** improved.
One of the main reasons **is** cost.

cards.title: Singular words that look plural
cards.body: **news, economics, mathematics, physics** and **everyone, everybody, nobody, each, every** take singular verbs.
examples: The news is worrying.
Everyone has a right to education.

cards.title: Plural words
examples: People are becoming more health-conscious.
The police are investigating.

items: The number of cars have increased.
The number of cars has increased.

cards.title: Use it in IELTS
cards.body: Agreement errors are among the most frequent in all bands below 7. Check every sentence that starts with 'The number of', 'One of' or 'Each'.
examples: The proportion of people who own a car has doubled.

practice.q: The number of tourists ___ risen every year.
practice.a: has
have
is

practice.q: One of the biggest problems [are] traffic.
Each of the countries [have] its own system.
Young people [is] more likely to use social media.
The quality of public services ___ (have) declined.

o: Mathematics are difficult for many students.
Mathematics is difficult for many students.
Mathematic is difficult for many students.
practice.a: Mathematics is difficult for many students.
The number of private schools has increased.

units.title: Tricky agreement: percentages, either/or, there is/are
units.summary: Percentages, fractions, collective nouns and 'there is/are' in data descriptions.

cards.title: Percentages and fractions
cards.body: The verb agrees with the noun after **of**.
examples: 20% of the population **lives** in cities. (population = singular)
20% of people **live** in cities. (people = plural)
Half of the money **was** spent.

cards.title: either…or / neither…nor
cards.body: The verb agrees with the **nearer** subject.
examples: Neither the teacher nor the students were ready.
Either the students or the teacher is responsible.

cards.title: there is / there are
cards.body: Agrees with the noun that follows.
examples: There is a large gap between rich and poor.
There are several reasons for this.

items: 40% of the energy come from coal.
40% of the energy comes from coal.

cards.title: Use it in IELTS
cards.body: Pie charts and tables constantly test this rule.
examples: Just under a third of the waste was recycled, while the rest was sent to landfill.

practice.q: About 60% of the land ___ used for farming.
practice.a: is
own

practice.q: There ___ a sharp rise in sales in 2015.
practice.a: was

practice.q: Neither the government nor the citizens ___ satisfied.
practice.a: are

o: Two thirds of the budget was spent on health.
Two thirds of the budget were spend on health.
Two third of the budget was spent on health.
practice.a: Two thirds of the budget was spent on health.
There are several reasons for this trend.

units.title: Parallel structure
units.summary: Keep items in a list in the same grammatical form.

cards.title: Same form in a list
cards.body: Items joined by **and, or, both…and, not only…but also** should have the same form.
examples: ✗ Exercise helps people to relax, sleeping better and lose weight.
✓ Exercise helps people relax, sleep better and lose weight.

items: Students should read widely, practising writing and to ask questions.
Students should read widely, practise writing and ask questions.
The job is interesting, challenging and pays well.
The job is interesting, challenging and well paid.

cards.title: Use it in IELTS
cards.body: Lists of reasons or solutions are common in Task 2; parallel structure keeps them clear.
examples: Governments can tackle obesity by taxing sugar, regulating advertising and funding sports facilities.

practice.a: cooking

practice.q: The plan is cheap, effective and [it is easy to manage].

o: Cities should build parks, improving transport and reduce noise.
Cities should build parks, improve transport and reduce noise.
Cities should build parks, to improve transport and reducing noise.
practice.a: Cities should build parks, improve transport and reduce noise.
Reading improves vocabulary, concentration and imagination.

units.title: Questions and word order
units.summary: Direct questions, indirect questions and basic sentence order.

cards.title: Basic order
examples: I met my friends at the café yesterday.

cards.title: Direct questions
cards.body: **(Question word) + auxiliary + subject + verb**. Subject questions have no auxiliary.
examples: Where do you live?
What happened? (subject question)

cards.title: Indirect questions
cards.body: After *Could you tell me…, I wonder…, Do you know…* use **statement order**.
examples: Could you tell me where the station is?
I'm not sure what the answer is.

items: Can you tell me where is the library?
Can you tell me where the library is?

cards.title: Use it in IELTS
cards.body: You may need to ask the examiner to clarify. Polite indirect questions sound natural.
examples: Could you explain what you mean by 'traditional'?

o: What time does the exam start?
What time does start the exam?
practice.a: What time does the exam start?

o: Do you know where is the bank?
Do you know where the bank is?
Do you know where does the bank is?
practice.a: Do you know where the bank is?
Could you tell me what this word means?
I bought a new laptop in Dhaka last week.

units.title: Punctuation: commas, semicolons, colons, apostrophes
units.summary: The punctuation that makes long sentences readable.

cards.title: Commas
cards.body:
Use a comma:
- after an introductory phrase or clause: *In 2010, …*, *Although…, …*
- before *and/but/so* joining two full sentences
- around non-defining clauses and in lists
Don't put a comma between a subject and its verb.
examples: In recent years, online shopping has grown rapidly.
Prices rose, but wages stayed the same.

cards.title: Semicolons and colons
cards.body: **;** joins two closely related sentences. **:** introduces a list or an explanation.
examples: Some prefer cities; others prefer villages.
There are two main causes: poverty and lack of education.

cards.title: Apostrophes
cards.body: **'s** for possession and contractions. **its** = possessive; **it's** = it is. Avoid contractions in formal essays.
examples: The country's economy grew.
The company lost its main client.

items: No comma between subject and verb.

cards.title: Use it in IELTS
cards.body: Punctuation is assessed as part of Grammatical Range and Accuracy.
examples: Overall, the most significant change was the rise in solar power.

practice.q: Tap the word that should be followed by a comma.
Tap the word that should be followed by a comma.

practice.a: its

o: There are two reasons: cost and time.
There are two reasons; cost and time.
There are two reasons, cost, and time.
practice.a: There are two reasons: cost and time.

practice.x: No comma between subject and verb.

practice.a: Overall, the most popular option was the bus.
